World.title: Six days to Osun election: 18 ‘killed’ as fears of more violence mount
World.content:
•Osogbo, Ede, Ife, Oriade, Ijebu-Ijesha, Ilobu, Ikire emerge as flashpoints

•Deployment of 15,000 policemen divides stakeholders

By Shina Abubakar

Fresh fears of further violence have gripped Osun State ahead of the August 15 governorship election, with the two major opposition parties, the All Progressives Congress, APC, and Accord Party, claiming to have lost a combined 18 members in the build-up to the poll.

.

The development has heightened concerns over the safety of voters, political parties and election officials as the state prepares for the governorship election, with the deployment of 15,000 policemen generating divergent reactions among political parties and civil society organisations.

Specifically, the build-up to the August 15 election has been punctuated by a series of violent incidents across the state, ranging from attacks on party supporters and campaign convoys to shootings and alleged assassination attempts.

Gunmen

In May, an Accord Party member, Kolade Eluyera, was killed in Irewole Local Government Area, an incident the party attributed to alleged APC supporters, a claim rejected by the opposition party.

The violence escalated on June 3 when the Accord chairman in Osogbo Local Government, Asimiyu Ajibola, was shot by gunmen and left receiving treatment in hospital.

Expectedly, the incident further heightened tension between the rival camps.

There was another reported death in Esa-Oke, where an Accord supporter, Ajayi Rogba, was killed during the period of heightened political activities.

The incident again triggered accusations, with Accord supporters linking the killing to political violence, while APC members in the area denied involvement and warned against politicising the incident.

Earlier, campaign activities in Ede, Osogbo and other parts of the state had also been disrupted by clashes, shootings and attacks on campaign convoys, reinforcing concerns that political disagreements were increasingly taking a violent dimension.

The scale of the violence has since become a major concern ahead of next week’s poll.

13 fatalities

For example, Kimpact Development Initiative said 44 election-related violent incidents resulting in 13 fatalities were recorded in Osun between October 2025 and June 2026.

However, the political parties in separate chats with Sunday Vanguard, presented higher figures in relation to their members’ deaths. While the APC campaign council alleged that 10 of its members had been killed during the electioneering period, the Accord Party said eight of its people had also lost their lives.

The parties have continued to trade accusations over responsibility for the violence, with each accusing the other of being behind attacks on its members.

Although the combined figure of 18 deaths claimed by the two parties has not been independently established as a single death toll, the allegations have heightened fears of possible reprisal attacks and further violence before, during and after the election.

The security situation has therefore become a major issue in the final days of the campaign, with stakeholders divided over whether the deployment of 15,000 policemen would help prevent violence or amount to militarisation of the electoral process.

10 of our members ‘ve been killed — APC Campaign Council

The APC campaign council said the number of personnel deployed was less important than the professionalism, equipment and capacity of security agencies to ensure a free, fair and credible election.

A member of the APC campaign council, Mr Kehinde Ayantunji, who spoke on behalf of the chairman, said the 15,000 personnel could be meaningless if they lacked the proper equipment and training needed to ensure a peaceful poll.

Ayantunji said: “Since the beginning of this campaign, they have killed nothing less than 10 members of our party in Ilesa, Iwo, Osogbo, Ijebu-Jesa and some other communities. It is unfortunate that human life is involved and there is no election that is worth the life of any human being.”

Speaking on the deployment of police officers, he said the party was not interested in the number of personnel but in the conduct of a free and fair election.

He said: “Most important thing is not about number, it’s about the professional conduct of the Police, capacity to protect the people’s vote, we are interested in free, fair and credible election, we are also interested in adequate security to ensure that the Accord members do not succeed in creating fear and apprehension in the mind of the people so that our supporters and party members can come out to vote for the candidate of their choice.”

The police, he said, “must do everything possible in terms of personnel, equipment, strategy and logistics to make sure that every vote counts in all the 3,761 polling units we have in Osun State. That’s our stand.”

Oriade, Ijebu-Ijesha, Ikire

On its part, the Accord Party said the number of policemen deployed might not be adequate considering the level of violence witnessed in some towns across the state, even as it called for more security personnel to ensure the safety of voters and votes.

The party’s Media Director, Mr Oladele Bamiji, said: “The Accord party has lost about eight people to violence since since the commencement of this campaign. We have seen killings in Oriade, Ijebu-Jesha, Ilobu, Ikire to be precise and even in Osogbo.

“The level of violence has been so bad, because people who have humanity at heart, who have blood running in their vein cannot be happy to loose just single person not to talk of eight. So, it is disheartening, frightening at the same time. People descend so low just because of electioneering, it is not a good way to lead people and it is a very bad moment for everyone.”

Bamiji also questioned the numerical arrangement of the deployment, considering the number of polling units across the state.

“I still don’t know the mathematical arrangement, we have very close to 4000 polling units in Osun State and we have four or five officers per polling units. To me, it is not so big, it is even inadequate. If a smaller state in terms of Local government like Ekiti, have more than us, I think there should be even more deployment. We understand that the Police are not the only security required for the electioneering, other security operatives will be around. I want to believe that they will compliment each other and have a peaceful election,” he said.

It’s militarisation of election, says Osun Masterminds

However, a coalition of civil society organisations in the state, The Osun Masterminds, expressed worry that the heavy deployment amounted to militarisation of the polls.

The spokesperson for the group, Mr Ayo Ologunde, said: “The deployment of 15,000 Police men for gubernatorial election in Osun signifies militarisation, the State and the Nation as a whole should have grown to a level where election should not be seen as war, even in a situation of war, 15,000 police officers is a lot.

“Police uniform create fear in the mind of the citizens, which causes voters apathy, now that 15,000 police have been deployed, some of them will start illegal checkpoint across the local government they are taken to, people won’t be able to walk freely at night for the fear of checkpoint in a state where there should be freedom of movement.

“Second, you have created likely security loop holes in the other states, because criminals are not resting, they know that on the day of election, there will be less policemen in the neighbouring state, hoodlums will want to take advantage of that deployment to commit crime in neighbouring state.”

In addition, he said: “Voting is a process of electing leaders, not a process of militarisation or to create undue fear.

“These policemen are not going to be deployed for free, they will be given allowances. Instead of giving them millions of naira as election allowance. Why don’t you use the money for infrastructure. It is a waste of resources at a time like this in the nation?”

15,000 policemen will stop violence

— Dialogue 365

However, the Convener of Dialogue 365, Mr Saka Waheed, backed the deployment, saying it was necessary to stop the violence and allow the conduct of a peaceful election.

Waheed said: “We demanded for protection, now we are having it. We cannot call it militarisation, the incessant killing in the past months show that if there is no enough security, there may be further killings on election day; it will be very unfortunate to allow miscreants take over our electoral process killing people.”

He added: “Let us have more than that, as long as our people will be secured that’s being proactive there can even be up to 50,000. We have an history of security deployment in Osun, even when those security came to harass our people during the Aregbesola time, despite that people still came out to say this is who we want as our Governor.”

Heavy deployment of security personnel driven by intelligence—ex-lawmaker

A former chairman of the House of Assembly Committee on Information, Mr Olatunbosun Oyintiloye, also threw his weight behind the deployment, saying it may be driven by intelligence available to the Federal Government.

Oyintiloye said: “The country faces security challenges, and the heavy deployment of security personnel to Osun State may be driven by intelligence available to the Federal Government.

“Such deployments are routine during election periods, and the state is familiar with them. There is, therefore, no cause for alarm.

“Nonetheless, concerns over rising incidents of extrajudicial killings remain. Security agencies must act decisively, while the government ramps up public sensitisation to encourage voter turnout without fear.”

With the election only days away, attention has consequently shifted to how the security agencies will manage the volatile political environment, particularly in areas considered flashpoints.

The competing claims by APC and Accord over the deaths of their members have also raised fresh concerns about possible retaliation and the potential for political violence to escalate before, during and after the election.

Stakeholders have therefore called for restraint among political parties and their supporters, while urging security agencies to ensure that the heavy deployment is used to protect voters and maintain peace rather than intimidate the electorate.

World.title: Ibadan meeting: Atiku, Obi, Kwankwaso still have opportunity for grand alliance — Ologbondiyan
World.content:
•2027: ‘Hungry Nigerians, not the opposition, will give Tinubu sleepless nights’

By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja

Few opposition figures have witnessed Nigeria’s political twists and realignments from as close a vantage point as Kola Ologbondiyan. A former National Publicity Secretary of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), he now serves as Special Adviser on Media and Publicity to the National Chairman of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Senator David Mark, placing him at the centre of fresh efforts to forge a formidable opposition ahead of the 2027 general election. In this interview, Ologbondiyan speaks on the prospects of a united opposition, the PDP’s lingering crisis, the ADC’s mission, and why he believes President Bola Tinubu’s biggest political test in 2027 will come not from rival parties, but from millions of Nigerians battling economic hardship. Excerpts:

Kola Ologbondiyan

You spent years shaping the PDP’s public communication. Looking at where the opposition stands today, with the ADC and NDC pulling in different directions, do you still believe, it can mount a credible challenge to President Tinubu before the January 2027 election?

I strongly believe so. And my belief is based on the decision reached at the meeting held in Ibadan among all the opposition political parties to look at that proposed grand alliance. The decision reached by the majority of the opposition parties was that, at the nick of time, they were going to pull together. I believe that the opposition political parties are going to realign and work in the direction of rescuing our nation from the path of perdition into which it is gradually drifting.

When Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso left the ADC coalition in May, what really went wrong? Was it a clash of personalities or disagreement over zoning or were there deeper issues Nigerians still don’t know about?

I think when the decision was taken to leave the ADC, my reading was that the decision was arrived at in a hurry. And I said this publicly because no point had been reached in the discussion to arrive at the position of leaving the alliance. And that is why I still believe that the opposition, if it can read the game properly, still has the opportunity for the grand alliance which the Ibadan meeting projected.

So, you think there is no real danger that both Atiku Abubakar and Obi/Kwankwaso camps will split the opposition vote again, just as happened in 2023?

What I’m saying, essentially, is that at the point at which the camps of Peter Obi as well as Kwankwaso left the coalition, no decision had been reached to warrant their departure. Because talks were still ongoing. I’ve also said that the best decision that can rescue our nation today is a government of national unity. And that this government of national unity was a disposition which the opposition political parties were working towards when they arrived at the Ibadan coalition’s decision, which is that all the political parties must come together, have one candidate, and work together. And I’m saying that I do not believe, I don’t want to say, that that decision has been foreclosed. I don’t want to say or hold on to the notion that that decision is dead. I believe that if the opposition political parties are determined to rescue this nation, the best approach is for all opposition political parties to pull together.

The PDP has elected a new national leadership this year? In your assessment, does the party still have the reach and strength to compete nationally? Do you think the PDP has lost too much ground?

I think my worry about the PDP is, I know you talked about the PDP today, but which PDP are you talking about? I think that is the challenge that I have. And I say so essentially because the role of the PDP was to serve as an opposition political party after losing power in 2015. But can we, with every sense of responsibility, say that the PDP as we have it now will serve that same purpose? I think the answer is no. And I want to leave it at that.

Many Nigerians argue that opposition parties become vocal only when elections are around the corner. But after the elections, everybody seems to go back to their various cocoons. Why has the opposition struggled to sustain pressure on the government over the economy, insecurity and the cost-of-living crisis?

I give it to the African Democratic Congress (ADC) coalition. Since it came onto the political scene about a year ago, I think the party spokesman Bolaji Abdullahi has been consistent in holding the government in power to its responsibilities. So I think that, moving forward, even if the party continues in that line, irrespective of what the disposition is after the 2027 election, I think it should emerge as a political party that has focus, that has determination, and that is going to serve the interests of Nigerians.

Both the ADC and NDC are still facing legal disputes. How confident are you that neither party will run into serious legal obstacles allegedly put in their way by the ruling party before the next general election?

I’m very confident, as long as the judiciary stands upright and continues to work in the interests of our democracy. Because if you look at the entirety of the matters in court, without being judgmental and without showing any form of disrespect to the judiciary, I think there are no issues. For instance, when you look at the issue of the party’s deregistration, and Nigerians are saying they are going to deregister it, I can say to you that I can’t see that happening because the law is very clear. I am not a lawyer; I never claimed to be one either. But it is clear what the law stipulates. It says that either you have won 25 per cent in the presidential election, or you have done this, or you have done that. The provisions of the law are not tied to one issue. You understand? And also, it is INEC that has the authority to decide which party to recognise or not recognise. So when you talk about deregistration and the whole issue, I don’t even look at the circumstances of everything that has happened. To me, the way I see it, it is just bringing the Presidency into disrepute because the law is very clear on how a party can be deregistered. You don’t just form a group suddenly, go to court suddenly, and then say that so-and-so party should not be registered. Then you have a Chief of Staff to the President, the face of the Presidency, who comes out and says that somebody (Hon. Leke Abejide) who left his party and took his party’s structure should go and scatter a particular political party. You just look at all this and discover that there is an arrangement to even bring the democracy that we all live for into disrepute and to a sudden death.

Beyond criticising the APC, what is that one policy proposal you believe clearly distinguishes the opposition and gives Nigerians a genuine alternative?

I think I would say that one distinguishing factor between the APC and the ADC coalition lies in the character of those who left the ruling party for the ADC. And I say so clearly because one thing that the ADC coalition has stood for since its inception, and also in the new turnaround of the political party, is the battle to ensure that democracy survives. I think that has been the focus. We object to a system that gives power to one man, to an individual, because democracy cannot thrive in a situation where only one man is respected and accorded the rights of a king in a democratic setting. So I think if you look at the ADC, that is the area of focus from the new turnaround of the political party.

Proceeding from there, what differentiates the ADC from the APC?

I will clearly tell you that the ADC has a vision of working with Nigerians to bring about a government that will work only in the interests of Nigerians, a government whose focus shall be to ensure that Nigerians thrive democratically and that the people benefit from democracy. Let’s go back a little to the Second Republic. When you mention the UPN in the Second Republic, what comes to mind is free education and an egalitarian society. When you mention the NPN, what comes to mind is agriculture, housing, and so on and so forth. When you mention the PRP, you think about the Talakawa. Come to the Fourth Republic. Mention any political party, any one, that gives you a clear picture of what it stands for. It is only the ADC now that can clearly say that it stands for democracy and is completely opposed to one-man rule. And I think that’s where we are.

Apart from the prominent opposition leaders Atiku, Obi, and Kwankwaso, do you see any other emerging figures Nigerians should keep an eye on after the 2027 vote and ahead of 2031?

I think what is common to the majority of Nigerians as we speak today is how to stop this government through the ballot. For it from proceeding beyond 2027. I think that is the task. And I would advise that the political groupings, whether in the PDP, the ADC, or wherever, the common denominator should be this: How do we rebuild this country? How do we rework this country using every democratic means to stop this suffering from continuing? I think that is the focus for now. I don’t want to go beyond that.

The President recently declared that he was ready to “fight to finish”, politically. How should the opposition interpret that statement?

Well, I believe that, for instance, the African Democratic Congress, where I belong, has already made its position very, very clear. But beyond that, I think there is a misconception in what Mr President said, and that misconception is on the part of Mr President. I think the President sees the issue of 2027 as one between him and the opposition political parties. The answer to that is no. I think the issue is between Mr President and Nigerians who are suffering, who are hungry, who have no money in their pockets. I think they are the people he should be prepared to contend with. And I am sure that, through their ballots, those Nigerians are also prepared to ensure that they vote against Mr President. So it is not about the opposition. It is a misconception to think or believe that the whole issue is between the President and the opposition political parties. Who are the people in the opposition political parties? They are Nigerians who do not want him to continue in office, and they are prepared, democratically, through their ballots, to stop him from continuing.

If you had one minute to convince an undecided Nigerian voter that the opposition; not particularly the ADC, the PDP, or any specific party, will win in 2027, what would you say?

Look, let me tell you. The facts speak for themselves. You don’t need to tell Nigerians anything. What are you going to tell them? That their lives are better today? The answer is no. What are you going to tell them? When the President came into office and said subsidy was gone and gone forever, those who believed him are now experiencing the consequences. There is no need to tell Nigerians anything. Nigerians are already telling themselves what they are passing through and what they are suffering. So, no, let’s not even go into that.

World.title: Insecurity: Scores of schools in 40 LGAs shut down
World.content:
•Three states worst hit as non-state actors disrupt learning

•Experts warn closures worsening out-of-school crisis, child labour, early marriage, radicalization

By Nnamdi Ojiego, Musa Ubandawaki, Umar Yusuf, Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo, Peter Duru, Ndahi Marama, Golok Nanmwa, Haruna Aliyu, Yauziyya Lawal & Maryam Usman

At least 65 secondary and primary schools have been shut or rendered non-functional by insecurity across northern Nigeria, findings by Sunday Vanguard have shown, with the closures cutting across dozens of local government areas and leaving thousands of children without normal access to classroom education.

Affected schools are spread across Sokoto, Benue, Plateau, Borno, Kaduna and Kebbi, while insecurity has also disrupted academic activities in parts of Katsina, Adamawa and other northern states.

The closures have been triggered by terrorist and bandit attacks, abductions, displacement of communities and fears of further attacks on pupils, students and teachers.

In some communities, schools have remained shut for prolonged periods.

In others, authorities have merged affected schools with institutions in safer locations or moved students to alternative centres to keep them in school.

The development has raised fresh concerns over Nigeria’s already severe out-of-school crisis and the long-term consequences of keeping children away from classrooms.

It has also persisted despite years of government and donor-backed interventions aimed at protecting schools from attacks, including the Safe Schools Initiative launched in 2014 after the abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Government Girls Secondary School, Chibok, Borno State.

The initiative was established as a partnership involving the Federal Government, the United Nations and the private sector to protect schools in high-risk communities and ensure that children could continue their education despite insecurity.

More than $30 million has been mobilised for the Safe Schools Initiative since its establishment, according to the Global Business Coalition for Education.

The Federal Government later introduced the National Plan on Financing Safe Schools for 2023 to 2026, with a projected investment of ¦ 144.86 billion.

The plan envisaged ¦ 32.58 billion in 2023, ¦ 36.98 billion in 2024, ¦ 37.15 billion in 2025 and ¦ 38.03 billion in 2026.

Yet, more than a decade after the Safe Schools Initiative was launched, attacks continue to drive children away from schools.

Sokoto shuts schools in 20 LGAs

Sokoto State has recorded one of the most extensive current disruptions. Schools in 20 of the state’s 23 local government areas have been shut following security concerns, according to the state government.

The Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Prof Ahmad Ladan Ala, said the closure followed a directive from the Federal Government.

He said schools across the state, including primary schools, had been closed indefinitely, with schools within Sokoto North, Sokoto South and Wamakko exempted.

The President of the All Nigerian Conference of Principals of Secondary Schools, Muhammad Ikililu, said insecurity had also disrupted boarding education in the state for several years.

According to him, boarding schools were moved to the state capital during the administration of former Governor Aminu Tambuwal because of insecurity in the North-West and Sokoto State in particular.

He said some of the affected schools remained closed.

Sunday Vanguard identified 14 schools affected by the current security situation across the state.

They include Government Secondary School, Tureta; Government Secondary School, Tangaza; Government Girls Secondary School, Bodinga; Government Girls Secondary School, Tambuwal; Government Technical College, Goronyo; Government Secondary School, Gudu; Government Secondary School, Gwadabawa; Government Girls Secondary School, Illela; Government Secondary School, Yabo; Government Girls Secondary School, Rabah; Government Technical College, Binji; Government Secondary School, Kebbe; Government Secondary School, Dange; and Government Secondary School, Shagari.

The governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in the state, Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, described the situation as a major setback to education and human capital development, saying the closures had deprived thousands of children of access to education.

Benue

In Benue, insecurity has forced the closure of numerous primary schools across Kwande, Gwer West, Guma and Logo local government areas.

Repeated attacks and displacement have made several communities unsafe for teaching and learning, forcing schools to close and families to move to safer locations.

Sunday Vanguard identified 35 affected schools in the state.

They include LGEA NKST Science Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA RCM Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA RCM Primary School, Igbur; LGEA Primary School, Chembe; LGEA Primary School, Iorza; LGEA NKST Primary School, Abeda-Shitile; LGEA RCM Primary School, Abeda-Shitile; LGEA RCM Primary School, Mchia; Shisho Unity Nursery and Primary School, Mchia; LGEA Primary School, Jootar; LGEA Primary School, Abiem; LGEA Primary School, Tyôgbihi; NKST Primary School, Azege; LGEA Primary School, Uzer; and RCM Primary School, Ikyule.

Others are NKST Primary School, Mbakighir; NKST Primary School, Kurungu; NKST Primary School, Audu; NKST Primary School, Annakaa; LGEA Primary School, Abur-Kpera; NKST Primary School, Anungwa; NKST Primary School, Gwatse; LGEA Primary School, Aman; LGEA Primary School, Gbeleve; LGEA Primary School, Ugwe; RCM Primary School, Poovule; RCM Primary School, Ibôr; LGEA Primary School, Kwagh; LGEA Primary School, Vir; LGEA RCM Primary School, Akombo; LGEA Primary School, Ubver; LGEA Primary School, Ageraga; LGEA RCM Primary School, Shausu; and LGEA Primary School, Mou.

Residents said the prolonged closure of schools had denied many children access to education.

Some pupils have moved to safer communities to continue their studies, while others have dropped out completely following the displacement of their families.

Borno

In Borno, renewed attacks have again disrupted schooling in Askira-Uba Local Government Area.

Sunday Vanguard’s correspondent identified two schools recently shut following attacks and abductions in the area.

They are Mussa Junior and Primary School, which was shut after the abduction of more than 40 students and pupils, and Lassa Secondary School, which was also shut following the abduction of more than 30 students.

The closures are a reminder of the long-running threat to education in Borno, where Boko Haram attacks have repeatedly targeted schools, teachers and students.

The state government had previously ordered the temporary closure of schools in Mussa, Dille, Lassa and Chul communities in Askira-Uba for security reasons, while students writing examinations were moved to Government Secondary School, Uba.

The Chairman of Askira-Uba LGA, Mada Saidu, had confirmed that 39 people, including three teaching staff and 36 students, were affected in one of the attacks.

Borno was one of the states at the centre of the Safe Schools Initiative following the Chibok abduction in 2014.

Plateau

In Plateau State, insecurity has disrupted academic activities in Riyom and Barkin Ladi LGAs. Sunday Vanguard identified seven schools in the two LGAs affected by insecurity.

They are Government Secondary School, GSS, Shonong, GSS Lwa, LEA Primary School, Hei-Gwe in Kwi District, GSS Fang, LEA Primary School Fang, all in Riyom LGA, as well as GSS Sho, GSS Barkin Ladi, GSS Ropp, Dogo Primary School, and LEA Primary School Dogo-Gashish in Barkin Ladi LGA.Berom Youth Moulders spokesman, Rwang Tenglong, said schools in affected communities were often shut for more than a week after attacks.

He said insecurity had continued to undermine education in rural communities because schools could not operate effectively when communities were unsafe.

Communities in Riyom where schools have experienced disruptions include Shonong, Lwa, Fang, Bangai, Tanjol, Darwat, Daku-Jol and Hei-Gwe Kwi.

Kaduna

Kaduna has generally maintained academic activities across most of its 23 LGAs, although some communities continue to experience insecurity. Sunday Vanguard identified two institutions in Chikun Local Government Area that have been affected by the security crisis: Bethel High School and Greenfield University.

Their names remain associated with some of the most serious school abduction incidents recorded in the state.

Birnin Gwari, Giwa, Chikun, Kajuru, Kauru and parts of Igabi continue to experience occasional disruptions arising from attacks, displacement and fears among parents and school authorities.

Kebbi

In Kebbi State, Government Girls Secondary School, Maga, in Danko/Wasagu Local Government Area, remains shut because of insecurity. The state government closed the school following a deadly attack and abduction of students by gunmen. The closure has further heightened concerns over the safety of boarding schools in communities vulnerable to attacks.

Katsina

In Katsina State, insecurity has led to prolonged closures of schools in several frontline LGAs. They include Batsari, Jibia, Kankara, Faskari, Sabuwa, Danmusa, Safana, Kurfi and Dandume.

At the height of the crisis, schools in vulnerable communities were closed as a precautionary measure to protect pupils and teachers. Teachers were moved to safer communities while thousands of children were left without regular access to their schools. Education authorities responded by merging many affected schools with neighbouring institutions in safer communities.

The arrangement has allowed thousands of pupils to continue learning, but several schools in frontline communities have yet to fully reopen because of lingering security concerns.

Yobe

Unlike Borno, Sunday Vanguard’s correspondent in Yobe reports that no school is currently shut because of insecurity except the College of Agriculture, Gujba. The state, however, remains deeply affected by the legacy of Boko Haram attacks on education. The College of Agriculture, Gujba, remains a reminder of the devastation caused by the insurgency. More than a decade after Boko Haram attacked the institution and killed students, the incident continues to symbolise the lasting consequences of attacks on educational institutions.

The wider crisis

The current Sunday Vanguard findings come against the background of a much larger national problem.

A 2025 investigation separately documented at least 188 public schools shut because of insecurity across six northern states: Katsina, Benue, Zamfara, Niger, Sokoto and Kaduna.

The breakdown put the number at 52 in Katsina, 55 in Benue, 39 in Zamfara, 30 in Niger, six in Sokoto and six in Kaduna. The investigation did not cover Borno, Yobe and Adamawa and noted that the actual number could be higher because some affected communities were inaccessible.

The figure provides a wider picture of the scale and persistence of the education crisis.

Maximum psychological impact

Security experts said attacks across several states suggest that kidnapping and banditry are evolving, with criminals increasingly targeting schools, public officials and vulnerable communities.

Security analyst, Sam Otoboeze, said the country’s kidnapping crisis was no longer driven solely by ransom payments but had also evolved into a strategy of intimidation designed to spread fear and undermine public confidence in the ability of the state to provide security.

He said the growing frequency of attacks on schools and isolated communities showed that criminal groups were selecting targets capable of generating maximum psychological impact.

Security consultant, Alfred Ononugbo, attributed the pattern partly to weak intelligence coordination and inadequate protection of vulnerable communities.

He said once criminal groups discovered that communities, schools and rural settlements could be attacked with little resistance, they were likely to return to such locations or replicate the tactics elsewhere.

Another security analyst, Masara Kim, described the situation as a major humanitarian and educational crisis, saying repeated attacks had devastated the education sector across the region.

According to him, several schools, particularly LEA primary schools in Plateau, have either been shut down, destroyed or abandoned after their host communities were attacked and displaced.

Kim cited LEA Primary School, Jwak in Mangu Local Government Area, which he said was completely burnt down during an attack on May 16, 2023, adding that the community remains deserted because residents have been unable to return due to insecurity.

He disclosed that terrorists at one point occupied the government secondary school, the primary healthcare clinic and a church in Hawk community after residents fled the area.

Kim further claimed that several children in Bokkos and Mangu were already out of school as of 2024 due to insecurity, warning that recent attacks, particularly in Mushere District where over 25,000 residents from more than 26 communities were displaced, may have pushed the number of out-of-school children in the two LGAs alone to over 40,000.

Education experts warn of long-term damage

The consequences of school closures extend beyond missed lessons, education experts warned. Chairman of the Conference of Polytechnics and Colleges of Technology in Nigeria, COREG, Dr Obini Onuchukwu, described the repeated closure of schools as one of the most damaging developments confronting the education sector.

According to him, prolonged closures disrupt academic calendars and make it difficult for schools and institutions in affected areas to achieve the same educational outcomes as their counterparts in safer communities.

He said students could not adequately compensate for prolonged classroom absence through private study at home, particularly where they lacked learning materials and proper supervision.

Onuchukwu also warned of psychological consequences, saying prolonged exposure to violence and insecurity could produce emotional distress, mental trauma and loss of interest in education.

He said attacks could also damage school facilities and disrupt the livelihoods of teachers, lecturers and other workers whose incomes depend on functioning educational institutions.

He warned that the situation could further encourage young Nigerians to seek opportunities abroad.

‘We will lose a generation’

An educationist at the Delta State Institute of Continuing Education, Eloho Arhogho-Okeren, said school closures could have consequences long after schools reopen.

“The closure of schools does more than halt lessons. It halts futures,” she said adding that some children who leave school temporarily never return, with many becoming involved in hawking, farming and other activities.

She called for alternative learning through radio and community learning centres, alongside school feeding, transport support, financial assistance and accelerated learning programmes.

“If we do not act now, we will not only lose a school year. We will lose a generation,” she said.

‘Out-of-school crisis could worsen’

Professor of Security Governance at the Federal University, Lafia, Dr Al Chukwuma Okoli, warned that prolonged school closures would worsen Nigeria’s already serious out-of-school problem.

Okoli said Nigeria has an estimated 18.3 million out-of-school children and warned that school closures in conflict-affected communities could further increase the number.

He said children who miss foundational learning opportunities face difficulties developing basic literacy and numeracy skills, leaving them vulnerable to functional illiteracy later in life.

He added that prolonged disruption would also reduce the future employability of affected children, increasing their dependence on subsistence livelihoods. The girl-child, he said, faces additional risks, including child labour and early marriage.

Okoli also warned of wider security implications, saying large populations of unschooled young people could become vulnerable to recruitment by terrorist groups, bandits and criminal networks. He described education disruption as a potential “threat multiplier” and called for urgent measures to protect and reopen schools.

The lecturer recommended stronger early-warning systems, rapid response mechanisms, community-based protection, radio and television lessons, digital learning, conditional cash transfers and school feeding for displaced families.

He also called for greater involvement of traditional and religious leaders in protecting schools and encouraging children to return to education.

Psychological and social toll

Speaking on the development, National President of the Association of Child and Learning Psychologists, Dr. Sixtus Unigwe, said effective and qualitative learning can only occur in an environment free from chaos and fear.

He noted that children thrive physically, emotionally, socially and intellectually when they feel safe and loved, stressing that without a sense of security, learning becomes impossible.

Unigwe explained that even when schools eventually reopen, the trauma from the initial closures is likely to linger. According to him, many pupils will struggle to concentrate in class, while others may develop truancy or avoid school entirely because it now feels threatening.

“There is every tendency that the fear that led to the closure of schools will still be haunting some children,” he said, adding that a learning environment built on anxiety undermines academic performance and overall development.

The psychologist further warned of broader societal consequences if the situation persists, saying children denied stable schooling may become vulnerable to gangsterism and other criminal activities including banditry and kidnapping.

He described the potential impact as “devastating on the entire society,” and called for urgent measures to restore safety in schools to protect the future of children in the affected states.

ActionAid seeks stronger implementation

The Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria, Dr Andrew Mamedu, called for practical implementation of the Safe Schools Initiative and stronger protection of children in vulnerable communities.

Mamedu said governments should provide alternative learning spaces for children displaced by insecurity and other emergencies.

He also called for stronger implementation of the Safe Schools Declaration, particularly at community level.

FG restructures Safe Schools Initiative

The Federal Government says it is taking steps to strengthen the Safe Schools Initiative. Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, told the Senate Ad hoc Committee investigating the programme that the Ministry of Education had established a full-fledged Safe Schools Department.

He said the ministry was working with the Office of the National Security Adviser, Department of State Services, Armed Forces, Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to develop a comprehensive national framework for school safety.

According to Alausa, the new approach would extend beyond physical security to include perimeter fencing, solar-powered lighting, water and sanitation facilities, school security personnel, technology and monitoring systems.

“Safe Schools is much broader than physical security,” he said, stressing that central coordination was necessary because the initiative involved several agencies and levels of government.

He said the Ministry of Education would provide policy direction, coordinate implementation with states and monitor the programme.

“Today, the Safe Schools Initiative is officially domiciled in the Federal Ministry of Education. We have also established a dedicated Safe Schools Department to coordinate policy, implementation and monitoring,” he said.

N144.8bn plan under scrutiny

The Safe Schools Initiative has received substantial financial commitments since its creation, but continued attacks have raised questions about implementation and effectiveness.

The initiative was launched in 2014 with an initial government commitment of $10 million, alongside private-sector funding. Subsequent fundraising pushed the resources mobilised for the initiative beyond $30 million.

The Federal Government’s National Plan on Financing Safe Schools for 2023 to 2026 envisaged a further ¦ 144.86 billion investment.

But the continued closure of schools has raised questions over how effectively the programme has translated financial commitments into physical protection for schools and communities.

The Senate has consequently opened an investigation into the Safe Schools Initiative to examine its financial and operational performance.

The inquiry comes as attacks continue to disrupt education in communities that remain vulnerable to terrorism and banditry.

Education experts warn, every school forced to close represents another setback to the country’s struggle to build the skilled, educated population needed for economic growth and national security.

Vanguard News

World.title: Tears, anger in Benue as 16 Otukpo attack victims buried
World.content:
Mourners weep uncontrollably as the victims are buried

By Peter Duru, Makurdi

Tears and anguish enveloped Efeyi community in Ugboju District of Otukpo Local Government Area, LGA, Benue State, on Saturday as residents conducted a mass burial for 16 persons allegedly killed by suspected armed herdsmen.

The victims were reportedly killed when the attackers invaded the community in the early hours of July 28, throwing residents into panic and forcing many to flee for safety.

According to residents, the assailants stormed Efeyi between 4am and 5am and opened fire on the community, killing 16 persons in what residents described as a brutal and unprovoked attack.

The incident has heightened concerns over the security situation in the area, coming barely months after another deadly attack that claimed several lives in communities within the same district.

At the mass burial, family members, community leaders, traditional rulers, political leaders and religious figures gathered to pay their final respects to the victims.

The solemn ceremony was marked by grief as mourners struggled to hold back tears while the remains of the deceased were brought to the burial ground.

A resident, Aboyi Owi, who attended the funeral, described the ceremony as one of the saddest moments in the history of the community.

He said, “The funeral was so touching. The atmosphere is full of sorrow, tears and anger because this was an avoidable death if those responsible for ensuring the security of lives and property were alive to their responsibilities.

“We do not know when our government will take genuine action to end the activities of armed herdsmen in this country. For as long as we allow armed herders to keep tormenting Nigerians, there will be no end to the mass killing of Nigerians by the criminal gangs. This is just the saddest day for the people of Efeyi community,” he added.

Prayers were offered for the repose of the souls of the deceased as mourners observed moments of silence in honour of those who lost their lives in the attack.

A Catholic priest led prayers at the ceremony before the coffins of the victims were lowered into the graves, amid wailing from bereaved relatives and sympathisers.

World.title: Police arrest Osun Commissioner over gunshots at APC rally; Adeleke kicks
World.content:
One of the injured.

By Shina Abubakar, OSOGBO

The Police have arrested Osun State Commissioner for Environment, Mr Mayowa Asejoorin, in connection with gunshots fired at the All Progressives Congress, APC, holds rally in Ilesa on Saturday.

Four persons were reportedly injured in the incident.

Reacting, Governor Ademola Adeleke’s campaign team, The Imole Campaign Council, described the arrest as a plot to silence Accord leaders in the state.

On the shooting, it was gathered that the APC supporters, during the rally in Ilesa metropolis, were attacked by some Accord chieftains, during which sporadic gunshots heard.

As a result, people sustained different degrees of injury, including a 14-year-old Ilesanmi.

As at press time, no casualty has been recorded. But the injured victims have been taken to the hospital for treatment.

An eyewitness, Kola Adeoti disclosed that the boy was at his mother’s shop when he was hit by a stray bullet on his thigh.

He added personnel of a security outfit based in the state, who escorted the Accord chieftains shot directly at the APC members which led to protest in Ilesa.

Why we arrested him – Police

Contacted, the Osun State Police Command spokesperson DSP Abiodun Ojelabi confirmed the report.

He said the Commissioner for Environment, Mr Mayowa Asejoorin was arrested in connection with the incident.

“Immediately the incident was reported, our personnel moved to the scene, cordoned off the area before some exhibit were recovered, which included expanded cartridges, Amotekun personnel caps.

“Also, Mr Adejoorin was arrested the scene and has been taken to the command for questioning as part of the investigation process,” he added.

Adeleke’s camp reacts

Reacting, the Imole Campaign Council spokesman, Pelumi Olajengbesi, told newsmen at the Imole Media Centre on Saturday, in Osogbo, that the manner of arrest is particularly disturbing.

He described the arrest as nothing short of a bandit-line abduction carried out under the cover of police authority.

Olajengbesi called on the Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu to reign in Osun Police Command and especially the Commissioner of Police, Ibrahim Gothan.

He added that Accord leaders and members will not be intimidated, and that the will of the people can not be arrested.

He said, “The latest victim of this alarming pattern is the Honourable Commissioner for Environment and Sanitation, Hon Mayowa Adejoorin, a prominent native of Ikiyinwa in Obokun Local Government Area of the state.

“The manner of his arrest is particularly disturbing. We consider what happened to Hon Adejoorin nothing short of a bandit-line abduction carried out under the cover of police authority.

“For some time now, we have witnessed a disturbing pattern in which prominent Accord leaders and supporters in Ijesaland are picked up by the Police on allegations that are apparently motivated by sinister political calculations, kept away from their families, communities and campaign activities, and thereby removed from circulation at a critical period of the electoral process.

‘APC desperate’

“The APC is desperate in Ijesaland. And rather than face the people in a free, fair and competitive election, there is a growing concern that these rejected political actors may be seeking to weaken the Accord Party’s structures by removing its leaders from the field.

“We are therefore deeply concerned that these arrests may be connected to an attempt to create an environment conducive to electoral manipulation in Ijesaland ahead of the August 15 governorship election.

“We therefore call directly on the Inspector-General of Police, Mr Tunde Disu, to urgently intervene in the situation in Osun State.

“Mr Inspector-General, the buck stops at your table. We call on you to rein in the Osun State Police Command and Mr Gottan in particular and immediately investigate the disturbing pattern of arrests involving Accord leaders, particularly in Ijesaland.

“We demand answers. On what basis was Hon Mayowa Adejoorin arrested? What offence has he committed? What evidence exists against him? Why was his arrest carried out in such a manner? And why does the Police appear increasingly willing to deploy its powers only against Accord political leaders at this critical moment in our democratic process?

“We demand the immediate release of Hon Mayowa Adejoorin, as we believe, there is no lawful and credible basis for his abduction and detention.”

World.title: Video: Olu of Warri rides electric scooter to inspect 5th coronation anniversary preparations
World.content:
Olu of Warri rides electric scooter to inspect 5th coronation anniversary preparations

As preparations for his fifth coronation anniversary gather momentum, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, took to the streets of Okere in Warri, Delta State, riding an electric scooter to conduct an on-the-spot assessment of the arrangements.

The revered monarch incorporated the inspection into his morning fitness routine, gliding through the community accompanied by members of his security detail. Residents and onlookers who spotted the royal father erupted in jubilation, cheering and hailing him as he moved freely around the area.

Olu of Warri Rides Scooter to Inspect 5th Coronation Anniversary Preparations pic.twitter.com/Kx47WrcHfE — Jeff George ™ (@jhon_odey) August 9, 2026

The public appearance has generated widespread reactions on social media, with many users praising the monarch’s accessibility, modern approach, and friendly disposition towards his subjects.

The Olu of Warri is expected to mark his fifth year on the prestigious throne with a series of high-profile activities.
