World.title: Solar eclipse to occur next week. Here is what to know
World.content:
Solar eclipse to occur next week. Here is what to know

toggle caption Edward M. Pio Roda/Getty Images

People throughout Europe and parts of the U.S. will be treated to a chance to see a solar eclipse on Wednesday.

People in Iceland, Greenland, northern Russia, Spain, and a part of Portugal will see a total eclipse, according to astronomers. That's when the moon passes between the Earth and the Sun, fully blocking the Sun's face. NASA says northern parts of the United States, including from Alaska to North Carolina, will see a partial solar eclipse.

Sponsor Message

During a partial solar eclipse, the moon passes between the sun and Earth, but the celestial bodies are not perfectly aligned. Because only parts of the sun are obscured, the sun appears as a crescent shape.

The partial eclipse is expected to begin around 1:17 p.m. ET in Washington, D.C. and have 4% coverage, according to NASA. That means up to 4 percent of the sun will be covered by the moon. In Reykjavík, Iceland, the total eclipse will begin at 5:48 p.m. local time , and in León, Spain, totality will begin at 8:28 p.m and last for two minutes. This will be the first solar eclipse visible from Spain's mainland since 1905, according to the European Space Agency.

For those who plan to watch either the total or partial eclipse, special equipment such as eclipse glasses or handheld viewers with special filters will be necessary to protect one's eyes. Regular sunglasses will not be effective for eye protection, even during a partial eclipse. Looking at the sun, even if for a short time, can cause significant eye damage, including burns and even permanent vision loss, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.

While the eclipse will give skywatchers a chance to safely marvel at the rare phenomena, some scientists will use it as an opportunity to better understand the sun. NASA says it will have teams using scientific balloons and a high-altitude jet to study how the sky when darkened for a short period of time impacts the Earth's atmosphere.

"From our unique perspective on Earth during a total solar eclipse, scientists can study the Sun's corona in a way we can't from anywhere else in the solar system," Kelly Korreck, eclipse program manager for NASA, said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

The next partial solar eclipse will be visible across parts of the U.S. on Aug. 2, 2027 – with totality visible from Spain, the Middle East and parts of North Africa. A total solar eclipse will be visible across parts of the contiguous U.S. on Aug. 23, 2044.

World.title: Tanker sailors still face danger in the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Tanker sailors still face danger in the Strait of Hormuz

An agreement over the Strait of Hormuz is still far away. Tim Wilkins, who works for a tanker industry group, says the ships stuck around the waterway are in limbo, and transiting is still dangerous.

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

Coming up this hour, join me as I learn about how a food delivery man in China has become a celebrated poet. And I talked to a sailor who is solo piloting his way around massive chunks of ice through the Russian Arctic.

But first, we will hear from an expert overseeing a different kind of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz because today, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council issued a list of demands that it says the U.S. needs to meet before the Strait of Hormuz can open. But this week, U.S. officials had said that talks were progressing to let the ships pass safely through the waterway. Meanwhile, hundreds of ships remain in limbo.

Tim Wilkins knows many of these ships and their owners and is following the situation in the strait. He's managing director of an industry group, Intertanko, which represents oil, chemical and gas tankers. Welcome.

TIM WILKINS: Thanks very much, Rob. Nice to meet you.

SCHMITZ: So what is it like right now for a tanker moving through the Strait of Hormuz?

WILKINS: The situation right now in the Strait of Hormuz remains severe. We are still having vessels being targeted by drones and by missiles, and the number of tankers transiting through the Strait is massively reduced compared to what it was pre-conflict. On Wednesday, Thursday and Friday this week, U.S. facilitated transits of about 11, 13, and then 15 were planned last night, so we assume that these have been successful.

SCHMITZ: You said that some of them have been targeted. Tell me a little bit more about that.

WILKINS: In the last 7 to 10 days, we've had a host of targeted vessels that have been transiting through there - either missiles or drones. Bearing in mind now, these vessels with seafarers on board, they're transiting. They've been given approval to transit through certain routes, so it's often unexpected and unplanned when these vessels have been attacked.

SCHMITZ: And what was the damage like?

WILKINS: The damage was pretty significant. In particular, we had quite a severe situation last week where we had a gas tanker which was hit and did -unfortunately, had to be evacuated. A fire did break out. This was one of the U.S.-facilitated transits that this gas carrier was being sort of transited through by night. So, you know, even with the U.S. facilitated, there are still risks, and it doesn't eliminate that risk of an attack.

SCHMITZ: What kind of presence does the U.S. military have in that type of scenario when a tanker is hit?

WILKINS: So U.S.-facilitated effectively means that those vessels have reported to the U.S. naval assets that are in the region. You might recall that the U.S. has a blockade in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz at the moment, so there are U.S. Naval assets in that region.

And what's happening is those vessels are contacting the U.S. They're transiting through what we call the southern or the Oman route. And those transits are being tracked basically by those assets. What we're being told is that those sort of naval assets are ready to intercept, and they have planes ready. But to all intents and purposes, those vessels are basically transiting and being monitored. That's basically the term of a U.S.-facilitated transit.

SCHMITZ: Understood. So we don't - it's not like a U.S. vessel is actually guiding a tanker through this area?

WILKINS: Not at all. And it's not as if you're going to have fighter jets overhead and naval vessels alongside or anything like that. Not at all. Yeah. It's very much a monitoring type of situation.

SCHMITZ: Got it. So tell me more about this route that the U.S. has carved along the coast of Oman.

WILKINS: There is something called the traffic separation scheme that goes right through the Strait of Hormuz, and that's been established since the late '60s. That's the international recognized strait. That, unfortunately, is one of the areas that is heavily mined right now.

SCHMITZ: Wow.

WILKINS: And what's happened is there's a northern route, which goes through Iranian waters - has opened up, and there have been sort of about single-digit, some double-digit figures of transits going through that Iranian route. And then there's a southern route, and it's the southern route that goes through Oman waters, which is being sort of termed as sort of the U.S.-facilitated route. The consent here is that you're sending these vessels through a route that is very close to the coast, isn't often used, hasn't been used really traditionally for 30 or 40 years for larger laden tankers. You know, these are 300,000-ton vessels laden with crude oil going close to the coast or being forced to go close to the coast.

SCHMITZ: Now, Tim, all of this sounds quite dangerous, and, you know, as a result, you mentioned that there are only 11 to 15 vessels going each night, and that's in comparison to around 150 vessel transits that we saw back in January, right?

WILKINS: Correct. Absolutely. So it's significantly lower. Let's take a step back. We are in a situation where the allied forces - those are the naval forces in the region - terming this a severe situation due to vessels again being targeted.

It's not a situation that's going to change overnight. There's a lot of things that have to happen. So regardless of this big negotiations that are going on at a high political level, there's some very practical issues that have to be resolved on the water, if you like, before you can get anywhere near that 150 transits a day again.

SCHMITZ: You know, as we talk about these big negotiations happening between the Trump administration and Iran, what kind of agreement would they need to see in order to make groups like yours feel safe to make a transit?

WILKINS: We've been calling for, first and foremost, mine clearance, to start. Start clearing the main sort of area of mines. And we know that there are, you know, French, U.K. forces ready to step in as soon as Iran gives the green light and allows them into that area. So that would be the first thing, mine clearance.

Ships should be assured that they will no longer be subject to attacks. That's something that absolutely has to be critical. So there needs to be that sort of assurance that the command and control system from Tehran down to those forces that are manning the Strait of Hormuz - that is critical. We want assurance that that is in place and vessels will no longer be attacked.

And then just some basic fundamental navigational safety points need to put in place. A single point of contact, for example, you know - who will manage the transit of these vessels? How will they manage transit times? Do vessels have to book a slot? So all these fundamental things that, at the high negotiating table, need to trickle down to members, the tanker industry, the wider tanker industry, before they will resume trade, you know, as they did before the conflict.

SCHMITZ: That is Tim Wilkins, managing director of the tanker industry group Intertanko. Thank you.

WILKINS: Thanks very much, Rob.

World.title: Ukraine mourns 'collector of souls' Oleksiy Yukov, killed recovering war dead
World.content:
Ukraine mourns 'collector of souls' Oleksiy Yukov, killed recovering war dead

toggle caption Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images

Oleksiy Yukov, a Ukrainian known as the "collector of souls" for his decades-long work recovering the remains of soldiers and civilians on the frontlines of war, was honored in Kyiv on Saturday after being killed by a landmine during a recovery mission in the eastern Donetsk region.

Yukov, 40, was killed on Aug. 5 when he stepped on the mine during an effort to exhume a body, according to a social media post by his friend, Serhiy Hnezdilov. "This is a great loss for me personally and for the people close to me," he wrote in a translation published by Kyiv Post. "[H]e gave names back to the dead."

Thousands of Ukrainians paid their respects to Yukov in an Orthodox Christian service in the capital. Before the service in Kyiv, Yukov was mourned and honored in his hometown of Sloviansk in Donetsk province.

Sponsor Message

Yukov was known for his tireless efforts to bring closure to the families of those killed in the war. In carrying out that task in 2022, he lost an eye and sustained a leg injury in a mine blast, The Associated Press says, but returned to his work even as he was still recovering.

As a teenager, Yukov became interested in searching for the remains on WWII battlefields in Ukraine, according to Ukrainska Pravda. After the Russian invasion and annexation of Crimea in 2014, he founded Platsdarm ("Bridgehead") to recover remains and provide dignified burials for the dead, the newspaper said. Through this work, he became known as a "collector of souls."

toggle caption Bram Janssen/AP

As part of a profile of Yukov, the newspaper quoted him as saying that he and a small group of Platsdarm volunteers would set off early every morning. "If it's a safe area, we survey the territory with a drone. We check trenches, craters, shell holes, belongings, rubbish bins," he said. "Then we divide the area into grids and search for mines and explosive devices using probes and metal detectors. We call in bomb disposal experts, who destroy or neutralize them. Then we carefully search the area for bodies."

Yukov and his team recovered not just Ukrainian soldiers, but Russian soldiers, too, as well as civilians killed as a result of the conflict that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives on both sides of the fighting.

Sponsor Message

Months into the full-scale war that began in Feb. 2022, Yukov told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that Russia "has caused tremendous grief for us."

Russia, he said "started a war against us; it is ruining our cities and killing our people. But we remain human even in these circumstances and gather their military's dead bodies."

In an International Emmy-award winning documentary about Platsdarm's work, titled Ukraine's Frontline Sacrifice, Yukov said that he believes souls are reborn.

"If the body is not yet buried, the body remains with the soul. And until it is mourned, until its loved ones let it go, it cannot be reborn – the soul wanders. And the war will not end as long as souls wander."

World.title: K-pop's global wave inspires Chile's next pop stars
World.content:
K-pop's global wave inspires Chile's next pop stars

toggle caption Rony Curifuta

SANTIAGO, Chile — Throughout this long, cold winter, an air of feverish anticipation has simmered in Chile's capital. This October, global K-pop sensation BTS will arrive in Santiago as part of their comeback world tour, marking the latest chapter in Latin America's growing embrace of Korean culture.

The group has already played sold-out dates in Mexico, while additional sell-out shows are scheduled in Colombia, Peru, Argentina and Brazil. Demand in Mexico was so high that President Claudia Sheinbaum contacted South Korean officials to explore the possibility of adding more dates.

From food and television to skincare and clothing, the Korean wave has found a passionate new audience across Latin America — and in Chile, it is being reimagined by a generation of young fans.

Sponsor Message

The phenomenon, known as Hallyu, or the "Korean wave," began spreading globally in the 1990s, moving Korean music, dramas, cuisine and beauty trends from niche interests into mainstream culture across the region.

But in Chile, young people are doing more than consuming the Korean wave — they are reshaping it. By adopting the core elements of K-pop, from energetic choreography and high-value video production to a youthful, colorful aesthetic, they are transforming it into something uniquely their own.

And now, a wave of homegrown, K-pop-inspired pop stars is building.

toggle caption Yuri Cortez/AFP

Q_ARE, a six-piece boy band, is producing energetic, fast-paced music that fuses lyrics in English, Spanish and Chilean slang with a K-pop aesthetic. Their videos combine retro video games, bright, flashing scene changes and colorful makeup — and they are amassing a considerable following.

Ahead of the launch of their single "FÚ" in May, they convened at a dance studio in Santiago to work on choreography for the song — stepping and spinning in loose clothing and high-top sneakers as they were put through their paces.

Outside, where salsa competed with reggaetón blaring from the different studios, the band explained where their inspiration came from.

"I entered the artistic world thanks to K-pop," said Seba, 22, one of the group's vocalists.

Sponsor Message

"But despite all the inspiration and influence we have from Korea, we're clearly not K-pop because we're Latinos. We've transformed it into something of our own."

The six boys — Seba, Jamin, Jota, Bin, Aiden and Fabi — answered an online casting call two years ago and, after a six-month audition process and rigorous training, the lineup was finalized. They debuted with their 2024 single "Try Again."

The group does everything itself, from songwriting to choreography, aesthetics to video design, and has its own fan group — the "Qniverse" — with members from around the globe. Q_ARE even went on tour to Brazil last year and has played at venues throughout Chile.

"We have fans from Singapore, a fan from Japan who always comments on everything we upload, many fans here in Chile, as well as in Peru, Mexico, the United States and Costa Rica," explains Bin, who raps and dances in Q_ARE.

"It's a bit crazy, really."

toggle caption John Bartlett for NPR

Occasionally, Chilean fans will take it upon themselves to explain the meaning of Chilean slang in their lyrics for other Latin Americans.

The "Korean wave" has now well and truly engulfed Chile.

There are now more than 50 Korean restaurants in Patronato, a small neighborhood that hosted the first wave of Korean migrants to Santiago throughout the 20th century. Many have Chilean owners who are capitalizing on the surge in interest in Korean culture, and others play music videos with their quick changes and colorful shifts on loop.

Like many Chileans, Valeria Vivar's connection to Korea began with a childhood fascination with anime and other Asian cultures. Today, she coordinates the Rey Sejong Institute in Santiago, a Korean government-backed cultural institution with centers around the world.

"We have different types of students," she says from a glass-walled foyer at Santiago's annual Korean cultural week. Around her, visitors sample Korean food, browse cosmetics, test their knowledge in quizzes and take part in K-pop dance contests.

Sponsor Message

The Rey Sejong Institute has about 200 students studying Korean — four times more than when it started classes in 2019. The center also runs a master's program in Korean Studies at Universidad Central.

"There are students who want to learn Korean because they like K-pop, so they want to understand the songs of their favorite artists. Others like watching K-dramas or movies in their original language. But we've also seen an increase in students who are interested in literature and Korean society."

With interest in Korean culture building more widely in Chile, Q_ARE is excited about where pop music is going.

"I personally feel that Asian culture in the arts is far ahead of Chile, but that also benefits us," says Fabi.

"We have the chance to create something new — hopefully, in the future, we'll see many more Chilean boy bands, and that's already happening. Many boy bands and girl bands are appearing, and we're super happy because we feel that we have been an example of taking that risk — others are deciding to take that opportunity."

World.title: Opinion: Europe's summer of heat
World.content:
Opinion: Europe's summer of heat

toggle caption Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images

This is Europe's summer of heat.

All 27 cities Italy's health ministry monitors, including Rome, Naples, Venice, and Bologna, are on red alert this week. People have been advised to avoid sunlight, sweet carbonated drinks, coffee and alcohol.

Imagine trying to avoid sunlight, fizz, wine, and espresso in Italy.

The World Meteorological Organization says this was the hottest June ever recorded in western Europe. And now the heat has returned.

Great cities, like London, Paris, Madrid, Florence and Rome, that draw tourists to museums, markets, theaters, and restaurants, are considered especially open and exposed. Those beautiful cities are sculpted out of brick and stone, and connected by monumental asphalt avenues which absorb the heat, and hold onto it at night.

Sponsor Message

Officials in France are just beginning to get hold of the toll of the June heat wave. They count at least 5,700 "excess deaths" during the swelter that climbed to 111 degrees Fahrenheit in the early part of the summer. Many of those who died were elderly, often alone, in a stifling house or apartment. Germany recorded nearly 100 drownings during the worst of the June heat, many of them young men.

Funeral homes have at times run out of space to store and prepare bodies for burial. Zouhaier Hertelli, a Paris funeral director, told the Associated Press this summer he has had to gently inform grieving families there was no room for their loved ones.

"Families are suffering," he said. "We have no solution to offer them, because the funeral homes are full. We are really facing a problem, a big problem."

It is hard for me to hear those words and not think of funeral homes in war zones I have covered, that have also been full.

Scientists say the steady rise of heat caused by climate change may ignite more fires like the ones that swept France and Spain last month and those raging in the U.S., Canada and across the world.

Sponsor Message

The European Investment Bank and the European Commission released a study this summer that predicts farm losses in the European Union will climb in the coming decades, with droughts, heat and storms damaging crop yields and stressing animals.

2026 has been Europe's summer of heat. Until, perhaps, next summer; and summers to come. Americans, along with the rest of the world, know that feeling, too.

World.title: Switzerland is a neutral nation but has more nuclear bunkers than any country in the world
World.content:
Switzerland is a neutral nation but has more nuclear bunkers than any country in the world

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

LUCERNE, Switzerland — From the outside, the Sonnenberg nuclear bunker looks innocent enough: its entrance is in the middle of a children's playground. But past the seesaws and swing sets, carved into a hill, is a thick blast-proof door that, when opened, exposes a narrow, well-lit tunnel that gently descends as far as the eye can see.

Sonnenberg Bunker guide Zora Schelbert walks slowly down the tunnel toward the main structure of the bunker, built in the 1970s, during the Cold War, to house 20,000 people in the event of a nuclear war.

"Back then, 20,000 people constituted a third of our city's inhabitants," says Schelbert. "So every third person in the city of Lucerne was once supposed to be sheltered in this bunker."

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

If a nuclear war between the U.S. and the Soviet Union were to happen, Swiss officials reasoned at the time, Switzerland — an historically neutral nation — would likely not suffer a direct hit. But it would be in the path of nuclear fallout from its non-neutral neighbors. So they supplied diesel-powered generators that had enough fuel to power this bunker for two weeks.

Sponsor Message

"So after two weeks, no more food, no more water, no more power," says Schelbert. "And today, civil defense also says that the duration of stay depends on what the problem is outside. And as we can see currently in Ukraine or Israel, this makes total sense because as long as it's a conventional war, people seek shelter temporarily and then you can leave again."

Instead of scrapping its nationwide network of bomb shelters after the Cold War ended, Switzerland doubled down and kept building them, guaranteeing every one of its 9 million citizens a bomb shelter space, just in case. The country has more than 370,000 nuclear bomb shelters.

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

"There were a couple of political discussions, especially in 2010, 2011," recalls Daniel Jordi, vice director of Switzerland's federal office of civil protection. "There was a discussion in the parliament to finish with the system."

But just as the national parliament was debating whether to scrap all of the country's bomb shelters in 2011, the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant in Japan melted down after a massive earthquake and tsunami. "And they came to the conclusion that it's good to have those shelters as a national reserve to protect the people in the real emergency," Jordi says.

Sponsor Message

That means every residential building in Switzerland is required to either build a bunker with proper blast doors and ventilation systems or developers have to earmark funds for a nearby bunker maintained by the state. Swiss citizens have to pay an upfront fee between $1,700 to around $3,500 for the maintenance and construction of these shelters.

In peacetime — which, due to its neutrality, is the norm in Switzerland — these bunkers are turned into wine cellars, saunas or, in the case of the University of Bern, storage.

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

History professor Silvia Berger Ziauddin shows off a foot-thick door made of reinforced concrete, the entrance to the nuclear bunker underneath her department's building. Berger Ziauddin, an expert on the history of Switzerland's network of nuclear bunkers, says bomb bunkers are rooted in the idea that this tiny alpine nation has, for more than a century, served as an island of calm surrounded by a sea of chaos.

"It was an idea already developed in [the] First World War, actually," she explains. "And then in the Second World War, it was the same island metaphor that was developed again. And in the Cold War, the island metaphor was transposed to the nuclear shelter."

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

Berger Ziauddin says the Swiss government cultivates this idea through the country's schools. Each year, she says, many students spend a week learning about these bunkers as part of a civil defense-centered curriculum, "where you have to draw civil defense shelters, you have to watch civil defense movies, you have to go to the shelter and eventually sleep in the shelter for one night," she says.

Berger Ziauddin says at the end of the week, kids present their drawings to their classmates. "But then also, kids also talked about their drawings and said, 'OK, in the upper level of my drawings there is destruction and death and chaos, and underneath, there is warmth and security and there is the shelter and the family and the pet and the mother working and the father is reading,'" she says. "And this imagery is very persistent for kids."

Sponsor Message

But Berger Ziauddin also says the reality of life in a nuclear bunker would be a far cry from how Swiss children imagine it.

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

At the Sonnenberg nuclear bunker beneath Lucerne, Schelbert, the guide, walks past the bunker's hospital with bright green walls — a stylistic holdover from the 1970s — to the fourth level of the bunker, a security station complete with three prison cells, all painted bright yellow.

"It's 16 spots for 20,000 people," she says. "And over the last two decades, doubts then were raised as to whether this would have been enough, given the circumstances that led to people entering. So that's why I think it's fair to say that the size of the facility and the problems that come with such a big mass of people, be it social problems, psychological issues, this can be considered one of the factors that contributed to downsizing."

toggle caption Rob Schmitz/NPR

And that's part of the reason why in 2002, Switzerland's government reduced the Sonnenberg bunker capacity from 20,000 to just 2,000. Its floors filled with bunk beds, a prison and hospital, all deep underground, have been repurposed over the years as overflow housing for refugees, asylum seekers and the homeless.

It's a use that has been criticized by organizations that help these populations. Some asylum seekers have protested against being housed here.

It has never been used for its original intent: to protect people from nuclear fallout. But the Swiss government continues to spend tens of millions of dollars a year to maintain it and hundreds of thousands of other bunkers throughout the country — just in case.

Esme Nicholson contributed to this report from Berlin.

World.title: The Women's Professional Baseball League makes its historic debut
World.content:
The Women's Professional Baseball League makes its historic debut

toggle caption Jaclyn Licht for NPR

SPRINGFIELD, Ill. — Three hours before game time, hundreds of fans swarmed the construction-lined, rain-soaked parking lot of Springfield's Robin Roberts Stadium. Some lived down the road; most hailed from across the country, and some had come from as far as away as South Korea and Australia.

Carol and Mike Studer, the grandparents of the New York Heights' first baseman London Studer, worried the weather would postpone London's start against the Los Angeles Queens and they'd miss their flight the next morning. One hour later, security parted the gates.

"Am I the very first inside?" yelled a teenage girl holding a baseball mitt as she rushed through a balloon-adorned entrance to be greeted by a custom bobblehead of Queens outfielder Mo'ne Davis.

Sponsor Message

Staff quietly hurried to tape falling signage to the walls, troubleshoot the jumbotron and cook burgers and hot dogs as rain seeped through the grated ceilings of the exterior walkways. Fans, meanwhile, made a beeline for the merch booth; within hours, sales were capped at two items per fan to accommodate demand. Underneath translucent ponchos, fans donned hats, sweatshirts and T-shirts in support of the league's four teams: the Queens, the Heights, the Boston Hunters and the San Francisco Firebells. Team loyalty was largely arbitrary, though; most said they were simply happy to support the athletes and to be present to witness the league's inaugural game.

toggle caption Jaclyn Licht for NPR

toggle caption Jaclyn Licht for NPR

toggle caption Jaclyn Licht for NPR

toggle caption Jaclyn Licht for NPR

Enter the players. The Hunters and Firebells, who would play the following day, wandered the grounds in full uniform. Many were greeted with hugs by their parents and siblings, who'd traveled from across the U.S. and from 11 different countries to witness their daughters and sisters play professionally for the first time. Girls and boys blocked the players' paths to ask for autographs, beaming at their parents as they showed off their newly signed T-shirts, mitts and baseballs.

The weekend marked the start of the Women's Pro Baseball League's inaugural season. Its four host cities — Boston, Los Angeles, San Francisco and New York — were chosen for their history of sports loyalty and market size, yet the opening season will run for six weeks in the geographically central location of Springfield, Ill.

The WPBL is the fifth professional women's baseball league in U.S. history, but Queens' third baseman Ashton Lansdell says, "We hope it's the fifth and the last."

Sponsor Message

Many of those signed to the WPBL began playing as young as 4 years old, and for many, their baseball trajectories stalled as they came of age and were told they were not allowed to compete alongside boys. But many of the players said the hurdle only fueled their determination to pursue the sport through other avenues.

Baseball For All, a nonprofit founded by WPBL Commissioner Justine Siegal, has supported young women in finding opportunities for organized play in their communities, schools and universities. Many compete in annual competitions, including the Women's Baseball World Cup, and have had stints in regional and seasonal men's leagues. A select few, including Lansdell, Firebells pitcher Kelsie Whitmore and Heights catcher Denae Benites, have even found success in the viral Banana Ball league playing for teams like the Savannah Bananas.

Most players, though, are juggling university studies or moonlight as bartenders, firefighters and architects to support their athletic dreams.

While opportunities for women's baseball have grown in recent years, this is the first time that these women will have a chance to compete and play together for an extended period of time. "I've been practicing so long on my own," said Boston's first baseman, Sabrina Robinson, during preseason training. "It's so different finally playing with other [professionals] in the same place now."

Meanwhile, on the third base line, 3-year-old Lenore Wooten took in the view of the field. "She'll never know this was never not a thing," said her mother, Jess.

World.title: Federal funds can't be used to give test strips to drug users, raising overdose fears
World.content:
Federal funds can't be used to give test strips to drug users, raising overdose fears

toggle caption Bebeto Matthews/AP Photo

Last year, Baltimore had three mass overdose incidents in the span of three months in its Penn North neighborhood.

In one incident, more than two dozen people were hospitalized after many were found unresponsive, lying in the streets or on sidewalks. No one died, but some came close.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Follow-up testing found that the street drugs contained high levels of N-methylclonazepam, a benzodiazepine that operates similarly to Xanax or Valium.

Like opioids, benzodiazepines suppress breathing. When they're combined, the risk of overdose goes up. And benzodiazepines don't respond to opioid overdose reversal drugs.

Afterward, the Baltimore Harm Reduction Coalition created test strips specifically for benzodiazepines. The group distributed them — along with test strips that identify other harmful adulterants, such as fentanyl, xylazine, and medetomidine — at clinics and neighborhood events.

Sponsor Message

The strips, available at no cost, can also be found in bars and spread out on street corners. People testing drugs mix a small amount with water and then dip a test strip into the liquid. The strip will change color if it identifies an adulterant.

"Nobody really knows what they're getting whenever they're getting stuff off of the street," said Candy Kerr, a spokesperson for the coalition. "Having the test strips available for the general public gives them the option to move slower if they're going to use whatever they're going to use."

But a new federal policy could make it harder for organizations such as Kerr's to give out the test strips, and they're worried that overdoses could increase.

In late April, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration banned the use of federal grants for distributing strips to the public and for some other harm reduction practices that have been credited with saving lives. Test strips have been used for nearly 10 years to identify adulterants.

toggle caption Scott Muacione

/WYPR

A letter sent to local health departments and nonprofits that provide addiction services explained that the Trump administration believes those harm reduction practices "facilitate illicit drug use and are incompatible with Federal laws."

Sponsor Message

According to the letter, grants from the Department of Health and Human Services also cannot be used for programs that support the use of clean needles or drug paraphernalia such as pipes, or to fund a type of specialized hotline that people can call while taking drugs, so someone is aware and can call for help if they overdose.

The Trump administration wants to focus more on other techniques, such as giving out naloxone, an overdose reversal drug available as a nasal spray, according to Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson.

"It is critical that federal funding provided by the American taxpayer goes to effective, common-sense solutions that have been proven to save lives and keep people out of an endless cycle of addiction and moves them into a life of recovery," she said.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/WYPR

The new policy does not prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase test strips for use by law enforcement officers, public health officials, EMTs, or other medical professionals.

That creates an important exception for government agencies that test drugs and send out regular reports on what adulterants are saturating the drug supply in certain locations.

Still, Yngvild Olsen, who oversaw SAMHSA's Center for Substance Abuse Treatment in the Biden and Trump administrations, says there is a substantial body of evidence that shows giving test strips to people who use drugs can change behavior.

"There's some people deciding not to use the substances, some people deciding to reduce, to use less, or take other types of precautions, including naloxone, and making sure that there are people around that can actually then help in the case of an overdose," Olsen said.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/

WYPR



Kerr said the best approach would be to continue to promote the use of test strips while also continuing to give out lifesaving medications like naloxone. She believes that working on all fronts has helped lead to Baltimore's decline in overdose deaths, which havedropped more than 40% since 2023.

Sponsor Message

Under the new policy, nonprofits will still be able to hand out test strips, but they will have to find other funding for that work, which Kerr finds worrisome.

"We've been making these strides forward because we've had these things, because we've been funded," she said. "We're going to have to pull money from other places."

To pay for the test strips, Kerr said, the Baltimore Harm Reduction Coalition will have to cut back on services such as giving out hygiene and wound care kits. But she said that option is better than risking another mass overdose in Baltimore — or allowing even just one preventable fatality.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WYPR and KFF Health News.

World.title: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Clad in a black bulletproof vest, a gun clasped to his hip, Tim Thayer gently pushes down the throttles of four 350-horsepower engines — and the 18,000-pound U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat jumps to life on the Detroit River.

Thayer is a marine interdiction agent, part of a team that patrols the waterways that make up the Canada-U.S. border in this part of the country.

He's assigned to the Detroit sector, an area that encompasses Michigan, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. The border with Canada here is entirely water — all 1,388 kilometres of it — which poses a unique challenge.

A peculiar quirk in the geography of the two countries is that Windsor, Ont., lies south of Detroit, separated by the river and connected by two bridges and a tunnel, with some seven million people crossing back and forth here alone annually.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat is shown navigating the Detroit River, near Windsor, Ont., on Aug. 4. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

On a warm Wednesday afternoon, Thayer scans south, looking toward the Windsor shoreline, his eyes searching for anything out of the ordinary.

"When we do our enforcement patrols out here on the Detroit River, what we're seeing is both people, narcotics and guns going back and forth between the U.S. and Canada," he said.

During the Prohibition era of the 1920s and '30s, the Windsor-Detroit corridor was the main route smugglers used to bring alcohol into the U.S. illegally from Canada.

While illegal activity on the Detroit River is perhaps not nearly as bustling today, the sheer number of recreational boaters who are frequently out presents a challenge for law enforcement.

WATCH | Trump's fentanyl claims aren't materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing: Trump’s fentanyl claims aren’t materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing | Duration 2:05 U.S. President Donald Trump declared a national emergency at both the northern and southern borders in 2025, citing the fentanyl crisis to justify tariffs levied against Canadian and Mexican imports. Ottawa, for its part, has committed roughly $1.3B in multi-year investments to beef up border security with the U.S. At the Detroit-Windsor border, the CBC’s Willy Lowry takes a look at how the U.S. handles things on their side of the fence.

"We saw how many boats today? And every boat could be a smuggler unless we stop every single boat," asked Kris Grogan, chief of external communications at CBP's air and marine operations.

"You have to use intelligence and partnerships to be able to secure this area up here."

Trump's claims aren't materializing

Just days into his second term in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canada of failing to prevent drugs, especially fentanyl and human traffickers, from entering the U.S., using the flow of drugs as justification to declare a national emergency and slapping 25 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977.

In February of this year, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those tariffs.

And while Trump has painted a picture of a porous and dangerous border, the reality is much more complicated.

In 2025, U.S. border officials in the Detroit sector seized more than 4,200 kilograms of illegal drugs, including nearly 15 kilograms of fentanyl, according to statistics provided by CBP. But the statistics don't reveal the direction the drugs were travelling.

"It's really not that big of a problem for inbound," said Lavarah Miller, a CBP watch commander on duty when CBC News toured a brand new American port of entry facility at the newly opened Gordie Howe International Bridge.

"A lot of the stuff that we actually get, we get a lot of it going out."

A view from the new American port of entry facility at the just-opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, which runs between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. CBC News recently spent two days with U.S. Customs Border and Protection agents stationed in the region. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

And guns, too, are travelling north, recent statistics show.

In 2024, 87 per cent of the guns recovered in crimes in Ontario were traced back to the U.S, according to figures compiled by Ontario Provincial Police. In Toronto, police say 88 per cent of guns recovered were illegally smuggled into the country.

"Firearms, for sure. But also, the United States is the middle ground for drugs coming up into our country from Mexico and South America," said Kelly Sundberg, a professor of criminology at Mount Royal University in Calgary.

While the flow of drugs and weapons between the two countries is primarily northward, Sundberg said, Canada still poses a threat to the U.S. — just not the one Trump continues to accuse Canada of.

"There is virtually no fentanyl getting smuggled into the United States, especially when you compare it to what's coming in from Mexico," he said. "Nevertheless Canada does have some serious issues with staffing [at our border] — we don't have enough officers.

"The officers we do have need to be better educated, better trained, better selected, better equipped. There needs to be a significant investment in the human side of our border security."

A tale of 2 borders

Canada's fentanyl czar — a role created in the early days of the trade war to try and assuage Trump's concerns about the northern border — has also pushed back against suggestions that Canada poses a major drug-trafficking threat.

In an interview with CBC's The House in June, Kevin Brosseau pointed to new data from CBP that shows less than half a kilogram of fentanyl was seized at the Canada-U.S. border in May, compared to 358 kilograms at the Mexico-U.S. border.

The total amount of fentanyl seized by U.S. officials so far this year at the Canadian border is approximately three kilograms. At the Mexican border, it's approximately 3,221 kilograms.

Despite ongoing political tensions between Washington and Ottawa, the U.S. border agents who spoke with CBC News over our two-day tour insisted the working relationship with their Canadian counterparts has remained unchanged over the last 18 months.

"Locally, we still have great partnerships with those agencies right across the water," said Tim Balkus, the patrol agent in charge of the Detroit sector.

Meanwhile, Thayer nods his head as an RCMP boat flies past, the Gordie Howe bridge looming large in the distance — a symbol of both how strong and strained the bond between the two countries is today.

World.title: U.S. booze might end up back on Canadian shelves, but have we lost the taste for it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Deb Anderson can't remember the last time she bought a product from the United States.

Like many Canadians, the 65 year old from Prospect, N.S., said she's been alarmed by U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated threats against Canada — and she's been boycotting American goods in protest.

So when she read on Friday that Canada was prepared to lift a ban on American alcohol sales as part of its trade negotiations with the Trump administration, Anderson says she felt disappointed.

"But just because it goes back on the shelves doesn't mean that sales are going to go back to where they were. The damage has been done," she told CBC in an interview.

Anderson says the "constant badgering and unfair negotiation practices" from the U.S. have "really give us a bad taste for all things American."

Anderson doesn't appear to be alone in her feelings: Sixty-nine per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy American alcohol if it goes back on store shelves, according to a Nanos Research poll published last month.

Support for a continued boycott of U.S. alcohol was highest in British Columbia, where 80.9 per cent of respondents said they were unlikely or somewhat unlikely to buy U.S. booze again if it's made available.

That was followed by 74.7 per cent of people in Ontario and 73.9 per cent of Quebecers who said the same, the poll found.

WATCH | Are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic?: Is the U.S. booze ban working? | Duration 3:31 With most Canadian provinces vowing to keep U.S. alcohol off store shelves in response to President Donald Trump’s latest tariff threats, CBC’s Eli Glasner asks: are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic or merely political symbolism — and an inconvenience for consumers.

Steep decline in U.S. alcohol imports

Industry sources with knowledge of Canada-U.S. trade negotiations told CBC News that the Canadian government was prepared to lift bans on alcohol sales as it negotiates possible concessions in exchange for U.S. tariff relief.

Trump has threatened to impose 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods on Aug. 19 if Canada fails to lift some retaliatory trade measures against the U.S., including the alcohol bans.

Those bans date back to early last year, when several provinces removed U.S. alcohol from the shelves at their respective liquor boards in response to Trump slapping a 25-per-cent tariff on Canadian goods.

Ivan Gedz, who owns the bar Union Local 613 in Ottawa, says his stockpile of American booze ran out two months after U.S. supplies were taken off the shelves at the Liquor Control Board of Ontario (LCBO) last year.

But Gedz says customers at the bar, which had previously offered a wide range of American spirits, didn't bat an eye at not having access to bourbon and other alcohol made south of the border.

Instead, the U.S. alcohol ban encouraged patrons to try booze they'd never had before.

"There's nothing I love more than giving someone an Indian whisky and they're like, 'India? I didn't even know India made whisky,' " Gedz told CBC News in an interview. "They're producing excellent stuff — it's just we don't get a ton of it."

A proposal to halt provincial bans on American booze was revealed Friday as negotiators race to reach a deal before new U.S. tariffs take effect on Aug. 19. However, a poll last month suggested 69 per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy U.S. alcohol even if it returns to shelves. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Changing tastes?

The need to seek out alternatives is something that was seen in other parts of Canada, too.

Quebec's liquor board, the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), said in its 2026 annual report that "fans of U.S. wines have turned to counterparts from other regions" amid the ban.

"Canadian wines, including Quebec wines, have gained popularity and now rank ahead of Australia's," the report said, adding that Austrian wines were also becoming more popular in "a sign that customers are curious and open to discovering new countries of origin."

Nicole Raufeisen is director of operations at Grape Witches, a bar and wine bottle shop in Toronto that continued to sell U.S. wines it already had stocked when the ban came into effect.

"We've slowly ticked away through those products. I think we're down to maybe just one or two different wines," she told CBC in an interview on Friday.

If the ban is lifted, Raufeisen says she expects customers will again reach for wines they enjoy from the U.S., such as fuller-bodied reds from California. "People will go back because those wines are good, that market share is well-trodden, so to speak, and the visibility there is high."

But she added that demand for American wines can also be attributed to trade barriers between provinces.

While nine provincial premiers announced last month that they would introduce direct-to-consumer alcohol sales between provinces, Raufeisen says restrictions on wholesale wine sales between provinces remain a major challenge.

"If there were no interprovincial barriers to the wholesale movement of wines, then it's possible that no one would miss any of the American wines," she said, noting that B.C. wines are comparable to those from California.

WATCH | Trump said Canada has 'nasty leadership': Canada has 'nasty leadership,' says Trump as he praises U.S. tariff policy | Duration 0:40 U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking from Las Vegas on Wednesday, praised his government's use of tariffs and once again mentioned Canada, saying, 'I love the people' but that the country has 'nasty leadership.'

Back in Ottawa, Gedz says Union Local 613 would probably bring U.S. booze back if the ban is lifted as part of a wider trade agreement between the two countries.

But he says he doesn't expect American alcohol to be as popular as it once was because many Canadians "have exposed themselves to products that they may not have tried" without the ban in place.

"I'm just hoping that those customers maintain their willingness for experimentation," Gedz said. "And you know what? If we stick it to the Americans for a little while longer, I'm cool with that."

World.title: Flight to Toronto cancelled over child standing on seat: Porter Airlines
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A flight bound for Toronto was cancelled Thursday evening after a young child refused to secure their seatbelt, Porter Airlines has said.

Flight PD444 from Victoria International Airport in B.C. to Toronto's Pearson International Airport did not take off as a safety precaution, a spokesperson for Porter Airlines told CBC Toronto in a statement Saturday.

The aircraft left the terminal and headed to the runway for departure but a young child standing in their seat did not secure their seatbelt, despite attempts by the accompanying parent and cabin crew, Brad Cicero said.

The unsafe situation meant the aircraft could not takeoff, so flight attendants opted to return to the terminal and disembark passengers, he added.

The time required to bridge the aircraft, deplane the child and parent, retrieve their baggage and refile paperwork meant the plane would have departed too late, according to Cicero, who said Victoria's airport runway closes at 12:30 a.m.

"We apologize for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day," Cicero said.

The aircraft departed the following afternoon, Cicero said.

World.title: The air travel industry was on the brink of disaster, but travellers are still taking to the skies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It seemed like airlines were on the brink of disaster heading into the peak summer travel season, with the Middle East war causing chaos and uncertainty, closing airspace in many areas and sending fuel prices soaring.

For weeks, headlines seemed to point toward a doomsday scenario. Fuel prices more than doubled in April. Europe was on track to run out of jet fuel by June, the International Energy Agency warned. Many airlines — including those in Canada — cut less profitable flights as a result. Florida-based Spirit Airlines fully shut down in May.

Despite all those headwinds, the industry — and passengers' desire to fly — appears to have rallied. Europe avoided its crisis by finding other sources of fuel , while passenger traffic has held steady, expected to increase by 2.1 per cent this year.

This summer even saw a new record: July 23 had the most global commercial flights ever tracked — a whopping 153,359, according to Flightradar24, a live flight tracker.

"What we're seeing is increased scheduled air traffic," said Ian Petchenik, Flightradar24's communications director. "It's really as simple as that."

Peak travel season

Total air passenger demand fell 1.7 per cent in June, according tothe International Air Transport Association (IATA). However, this was a smaller drop than the preceding months, and much of it was concentrated in the Middle East, which saw a 13.9 per cent fall year over year.

There isn't one single explanation for the July record, experts told CBC News. But it was likely fuelled by demand from the Northern Hemisphere, Newsweek reported , as airlines have been deploying maximum capacity for the season when travel typically peaks.

The last Thursday or Friday of July is usually the busiest, says Petchenik, as many see it as the peak of the summer season, just before school begins in August in much of the U.S.

For this summer in particular, he says, many of those flights were likely booked well in advance.

LISTEN | Canada's domestic tourism boom: The Current 18:53 Why Canadian tourism is booming At a time when the overall economy is sluggish, the Canadian tourism sector is bucking the trend and projected to grow by 6% in 2026. We hear from some innovative Canadian travel businesses that are cashing in and from tourism and hospitality professor Wayne Smith about what is driving the growth — and what it would take to build on it.

"A lot of people looking at the state of the world … before prices really spiked and saying, 'Maybe we should book now to get ahead of any incoming price increases.' "

Canadian commercial flights increased over the summer, as well, by Flightradar24's count, rising by 16 per cent between April 1 and July 23 to hit 5,558. Global commercial flights increased by 11 per cent that same time period.

But the number of flights alone doesn't always paint the full picture, said Amra Durakovic of Flight Centre Travel Group Canada. That's because our total annual commercial flight count remains 20 per cent below 2019, she said, citing data from analytics firm Cirium.

The global increase in flights is likely driven by large, emerging economies like China and India, which are increasing their flights as their markets grow.

However, countries with more established flight industries — like Canada — have instead increased the size of the average plane, while phasing out smaller ones. That means more people are served in the end.

Tourists take selfies with a reflection of the Eiffel Tower in the Champ-de-Mars garden in Paris on July 28. Canadians heading to Europe this summer have tended to book flights last minute, adopting what industry experts refer to as a wait-and-see approach. (Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images)

Where Canadians are going

On July 23, most Canadian travel was domestic, accounting for more than a third of all bookings, according to Flight Centre data.

Durakovic says her firm hasn't seen that happen since before the COVID-19 pandemic, and she notes it's likely that people are rerouting trips that originally would have been to the U.S.

Still, the U.S. was the second most popular destination that day, at 19 per cent, followed by European countries like the U.K., Italy and Spain, at 18 per cent combined.

Durakovic also noted an interesting trend among Canadians heading to Europe: They tended to book their flights last minute, as opposed to the typical approach of booking in advance.

"They've adopted what we refer to as a wait-and-see approach," said Durakovic, who attributed the trend to ongoing uncertainty around factors impacting the industry, like fuel costs and contract disputes.

Meanwhile, summer travel through Flight Centre Canada to Japan is up 37 per cent year over year — a significant sum considering the East Asian country is a long-haul flight away, at a time when cost remains a priority for many.

Notably, that demand is extending into the winter months, Durakovic says, as Canadians are finding it can be more affordable to ski in Japan, largely due to the weak yen.

"That's what is largely driving a lot of Canadians' travel decisions is where are they going to find the best value?"

Tourists ride on horses at the fifth station of Mount Fuji in Fujiyoshida, Yamanashi prefecture on July 23, 2026. Japan has become a popular tourist destination for travellers seeking good value for their money. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images)

What lies ahead

So far, the Middle East war hasn't seemed to significantly affect summer plans outside that region. But that may change the longer it goes on, alongside events like the recent WestJet strike , for example, which can erode confidence in travelling.

"I think that the more uncertainty there is and the higher prices rise … we will see a pullback in demand," said Petchenik of Flightradar24.

He says that could also trigger a shift to more local travel: "You know, 'I am buying a ticket, but … I'm flying somewhere where the prices are reasonable and I have certainty that my trip isn't going to be affected by world events outside of my control.' "

WATCH | How the war affected flight prices in March: How is war in the Middle East affecting flight prices for Canadians? | Duration 3:37 The costs of the war in the Middle East keep adding up as gas and diesel prices have risen sharply around the world; the cost of jet fuel has also increased. For people planning trips, it can be a scramble to find something less expensive. McKenzie McMillan from The Travel Group Ltd. explains how the war is affecting flights and by how much.

As for ticket prices, expect them to continue increasing, according to IATA. Airlines are still profitable, but their margins are under severe pressure due to fuel prices and with few ways remaining for them to cut costs.

Durakovic says she still expects demand to remain high in the near future.

"Look, it's a lot, but when we travel, we all love it, right?" she said, noting that people are generally willing to cut other costs to afford travel. "It says a lot about how important travelling is."

World.title: 'I woke up and I had lost the baby': Miscarriages in Gaza spike amid harsh conditions, UN report finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a small, dark room off the side of the morgue in the Nasr Medical Complex in central Gaza, about a dozen tiny white shrouds are arranged on a metal table.

These are the remains of recent miscarriages.

The white cloths are labelled with the term of pregnancy and the date of the miscarriage as well as sometimes a name.

Shrouds containing the remains of recent miscarriages are kept in a small room of the morgue at Nasr Medical Complex in central Gaza. UNFPA officials say the reported rate of miscarriages in Gaza for the first six months of 2026 was more than three times higher than in the second half of 2025. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

Dr. Ahmed Al-Farra, head of pediatrics at the hospital, told CBC News late last month that the miscarriage situation is alarming.

"The percentage increased nearly three-fold in comparison with the percentage from before the war," he told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife.

There have been nearly "4,000 pregnancy losses" recorded as miscarriages in the enclave between January and June 2026, a rate that's more than three times higher than in the second half of 2025, according to a statement provided by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

This number doesn’t include instances where a miscarriage happened outside the hospital.

WATCH | Doctor says living conditions in Gaza lead to miscarriages: Nearly 4,000 miscarriages happened in Gaza between January and June | Duration 1:42 Ahmed Al-Farra says the high rate of miscarriages is due to a lack of access to clean water, nutritious food, shelter and living in a high-stress environment in Gaza.

What pregnant women in Gaza endure

UNFPA's statement notes that pregnant women in the strip "endure severe food insecurity, malnutrition, repeated displacement, sustained psychological trauma and overcrowded and unsanitary living conditions."

The organization says interruptions to prenatal care and limited access to essential health-care services like diagnostics, medicine and emergency obstetric procedures "leave complications undetected or untreated."

In its statement, the organization notes that more analysis is needed to better understand the reasons behind the increase in miscarriages. It has commissioned a report to further analyze conditions pregnant women are experiencing on the ground in Gaza. That report is due out in about two months.

A July report published by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says sexual and reproductive health indicators "continue to deteriorate" across Gaza during the first six months of 2026.

"Nearly 74 per cent of pregnancy losses occurred during the first trimester, while 57.1 per cent of pregnant women were anemic," it noted. These numbers "highlight the worsening health and nutritional status of women in Gaza."

According to the UNFPA, the number of miscarriages recorded in Gaza doesn’t include instances where a miscarriage happened outside the hospital. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

Fear, anxiety contributing factors: Doctor

Al-Farra's experiences at the Nasr Medical Complex align with these numbers.

He says there are many factors that contribute to rising miscarriages, including the inhumane living conditions pregnant women face, such as extreme temperatures, the struggle to find food and water and the constant displacement of their families. He says they also contribute to fear and anxiety.

"They’re afraid," he said. "They are suffering a lot."

Eman Abu Fasifsa, 38, lives in a makeshift room at a UN-run school in central Gaza with her five children. Her walls are pieces of tarp held up with rope. She recently went through a miscarriage after being pregnant with her sixth child.

"The day of my miscarriage there was a very, very strong explosion," she said. "I was so scared, and that morning I woke up and I had lost the baby."

Abu Fasifsa says she also spent her pregnancy carrying heavy water jugs and had a hard time finding food, which she thinks also contributed to the miscarriage.

A displaced Palestinian woman carries containers of water last month in Gaza City. Though food insecurity in Gaza is easing, human rights groups say finding enough to eat and drink in the enclave is still a struggle. (Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)

Aid needs still not being met

In Gaza, food insecurity has eased, according to a recent OCHA report , which also notes there's a real risk that those gains could be reversed as aid coverage has declined since February 2026, based on the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification analysis .

On Thursday, Israel's Co-ordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) wrote in a post to X that it has co-ordinated the entry of more than two million tons of food "along with other essential humanitarian aid" into the enclave.

"The constant flow of food has contributed to reduced market prices, as markets across Gaza offer a variety of fresh fruits, vegetables, meat and dairy products," the post said.

But for Abu Fasifsa, finding that food for herself and her children is still a struggle.

"There is no good food, no clean water, no safe place," she said. "We can only save food for one day. The situation is very difficult, really."

And that's true for families throughout Gaza, despite the ceasefire, according to the UNFPA's statement.

"Nearly 90 per cent of the population remains displaced," the statement said. "Humanitarian access and the movement of essential goods remain constrained."

Gaza, it says, "has not moved from emergency response to recovery."

Abu Fasifsa, who lives in a makeshift run school in central Gaza with her five children, says after her recent miscarriage, she isn't considering getting pregnant again. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

Back at the UN school where she lives, Abu Fasifsa sits to chat with her sons as the sun begins to set.

She says she isn’t considering getting pregnant again because of how difficult her living conditions are at the moment. But she still longs for the baby she lost, as well as the life she had before the war.

"It was my dream to have the child with me today, with my children," she said.

World.title: Coyote pup curls up in Toronto woman's bed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Imagine finding a coyote in your bed. That’s exactly what happened to Alice Kent, who told CBC’s Metro Morning how the animal got inside her Christie Pits home — and what happened next.

Every Tuesday evening, Alice Kent leaves the back door of her Christie Pits home open for her cleaner.

But one day, after chatting and welcoming the cleaner into her house, Kent realized that the open door also let in an unexpected furry friend.

"She goes upstairs to start on her cleaning and she very calmly comes back down half of the stairs and says to me, 'I think there's a fox in your bedroom,'" said Kent.

The "fox" was actually a baby coyote she said was laying on the mattress of the house's master bedroom.

"I thought maybe she was playing a prank or she left a stuffed animal out for me or something," said Kent. "I went up and expecting to see something cute ... I looked into my room and there was a coyote on my bed."

In recent years, Toronto has experienced a spike in encounters between people and coyotes. Since 2020, there have been nine incidents where people in Toronto have been bitten by coyotes, according to statistics provided by city staff. In February 2025, Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik put forward an urgent action plan.

This June, a child was attacked and taken to hospital in Whitby, Ont., followed by a two-year-old in July, also in Whitby. The recent encounters have sparked public outcry and led to a debate about population control.

For Kent, while she originally thought the pup was cute, after the reality of the situation set in, those feelings shifted.

"It was immediately just a lot of thoughts and feelings about danger for my kids or my cleaner or myself," said Kent. "If it was cornered or if it was in a place that had no escape, it might get aggressive."

Adding to the situation, the coyote pup had mange, a skin condition leading to scabs, itchy skin and missing patches of fur.

Realizing the immediacy, Kent called both 911 and the Toronto Wildlife Center.

Catching and treating the baby coyote

Close coyote encounters like this are nothing new for the Christie Pits neighborhood.

"There is a lot of feeding still going on of coyotes in this area," said Nathalie Karvonen, executive director of the Toronto Wildlife Center.

"That is a terrible thing to do for coyotes because it changes their behavior and it does make them less afraid of people and less afraid of houses," she said.

When the police and wildlife response team arrived, Karvonen said the pup was found hiding under the bed.

The Toronto Wildlife Center, Toronto Police Service and some of Kent's neighbors responded to the scene. (Submitted by Alice Kent)

All the team had to do was pull the pup out from under the bed.

"This family [of coyotes] is known to us because they are all sick with social sarcoptic mange and we have been trying to track them down," said Karvonen.

After apprehending the pup from Kent's home, Karvonen says her team did a quick check of the condition of the coyote and did a treatment at the location. They then released it into the area."

Kent said that a few weeks before the incident, she had noticed three coyote pups often sitting on her back deck.

She said she would scare them away from her property — advice given by the Wildlife Center.

According to Karvonen, the best ways to deal with unwanted coyotes is to remove food sources like pet food, supervise cats or small dogs, and make loud noises.

"On the one hand we want to tell people if you're scared of them this is what you can do. But then we also want to kind of reinforce that there isn't really any reason to be afraid of them," she said.

The Toronto Wildlife Centre only tracks coyotes that are reported as 'sick' in Toronto.

The question of exact numbers hangs in the air: when asked about how many coyotes she thinks are roaming the city, Karvonen said there would need to be a multi-million dollar study to get a true idea of the scale.

World.title: Canada, U.S. shadow Chinese research ships in the Arctic as concern grows over Snow Dragons' presence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Both Canada and the U.S. have been quietly shadowing two Chinese icebreaking research ships in Arctic waters off Alaska over the last couple of weeks.

The Xue Long (Snow Dragon) and Xue Long (Snow Dragon) 2 sailed north through the U.S. exclusive economic zone in the Bering Sea in July, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

The appearance of Chinese research ships every summer in the Arctic Ocean over the last few years has been a subject of growing concern among security and defence officials.

Data compiled by Steffan Watkins, an independent research consultant and ship tracker, shows a Royal Canadian Air Force CP-140 surveillance plane has been operating out of Alaska since early July.

The Department of National Defence confirmed Friday that the plane has been watching the activities of the two Chinese vessels in tandem with the Americans.

"The Canadian Joint Operations Command is actively monitoring maritime traffic in the Arctic, including the vessels Xue Long and Xue Long 2," defence spokesperson Cheryl Forrest said in a written statement.

"Both vessels are currently operating outside of Canada’s exclusive economic zone," Forrest added, referring to the area of ocean beyond territorial waters where the country has sovereign rights to resources and jurisdiction over activities like research and protection of the marine environment.

WATCH | From 2025: Canada monitors Chinese research vessel: Why is the Canadian military closely monitoring a Chinese research vessel? | Duration 3:48 The Canadian military and possibly the Coast Guard are closely monitoring a Chinese research vessel that has breached Arctic waters for the second year in a row. CBC's Murray Brewster says the Coast Guard was 'following a parallel course' of the vessel, despite denying any 'shadowing.'

Last year, the Canadian military began a focused effort to better monitor northern waters and co-ordinate with allies in the Pacific Ocean, including the Bering Sea off Alaska, under the banner of Operation Latitude.

The Royal Canadian Navy has committed the frigate HMCS Ottawa and the Arctic offshore ships HMCS Max Bernays and HMCS Robert Hampton Gray, in addition to the air force's surveillance aircraft.

The defence department says Canadian Special Operations Forces Command personnel and the icebreaker CCGS Des Groseilliers are also taking part.

Buoys can track submarine activity

When asked about the Chinese ships on Thursday, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the Canadian military actively monitors the country's waters.

China, which has declared itself a near-Arctic state, has repeatedly said the deployment of its icebreakers to the region is strictly for peaceful scientific research, environmental monitoring and global climate change studies.

Both research ships, however, have been known to deploy advanced sonar and telemetry buoys. Western defence officials say these devices not only track environmental changes and undersea topography, but are also useful in tracking submarine activity.

"Those research ships could do so many different things," said Richard Shimooka, a defence researcher at the Ottawa-based Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

There are no major international undersea fibre-optic cables in the Bering Sea region, but there is a regional subsea network vital to Alaska. Shimooka said he wonders how much time the Chinese are devoting to mapping that grid, in the same way the Russians are doing in the Baltic Sea and the North Atlantic.

People attend the launch ceremony of China's first domestically built polar icebreaker Xue Long 2 (Snow Dragon 2) at a shipyard in Shanghai on Sept. 10, 2018. (Reuters)

Canada, Shimooka said, is playing an increasingly important role in the western Pacific at a time when the U.S. Navy is occupied with the Iran war. But, he cautioned, given the age of the Canadian navy's frigates and coast guard ships, the country can't do much more than it's currently doing.

"I wouldn't say we're stressed, but it certainly is kind of reaching the limits that we can sustain comfortably given the age of the Halifax class," he said.

Described as the "backbone of the Royal Canadian Navy," the Halifax-class patrol frigates are now between 30 and 40 years old.

'Testing our capabilities to respond'

Members of the House of Commons defence committee travelled to the Arctic in mid- to late July and Conservative defence critic James Bezan left convinced that the region needs more surveillance.

"We know we've had to have more assets in the Arctic to ensure that we are monitoring the movements of the People's Republic of China as they continue to increase their interest in our Arctic," said Bezan, who noted that China has also been increasingly co-operating and co-ordinating its air activity in the Arctic with Russia.

"They are definitely challenging and testing our capabilities to respond to these incursions."

The federal government has begun investing heavily in the construction of new destroyers and begun the process of acquiring Arctic-capable submarines. It also plans to deploy an undersea network of sensors.

Bezan said time is of the essence because the country's sovereignty is at stake.

"Russia and China do not recognize our maritime claims" in the Far North, including the Northwest Passage, Bezan said.

"So, we need to be investing in the Arctic. When you look at the vast amounts of resources, a high percentage of energy resources that are locked in the Arctic, including in the Beaufort Sea, we have to do more to protect it and defend against these adversaries."

World.title: Colby Cosh: Supreme Court to decide which comes first — Crown oath or Sikh faith
World.content:
Article content

Most of the other provinces have abandoned the explicit oath of constitutional allegiance for lawyers, or made that oath optional, although that’s kind of a funny thing to do with an oath if you think about it. My six or seven readers who are fellow atheist-monarchists ought to recognize that the “Wirring Question” is a legitimately hairy one. The oath of Canadian citizenship, like the oath in the statute governing Alberta lawyers, still requires a declaration of “true allegiance” to the King of Canada. Whenever that oath has been challenged in court, so far, it has been upheld on the grounds that this statement — while seeming to demand obedience to a living, breathing human being — is really just a symbolic commitment to the Constitution. (A republican, I suppose, can take such an oath in good conscience because it is a pledge to the King and his “successors,” who might not be monarchs at all.)
